newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister warns of dangers of power-sharing.
newsitem.headline: French minister warns of dangers of power-sharing.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette warned on Wednesday that power-sharing between a leftist government and conservative President Jacques Chirac would harm French interests in Europe and within NATO.
Should the left win France's May 25-June 1 parliamentary election, "one can easily see a danger of France growing weaker," de Charette warned.
"That would lead to difficult and complicated negotiations in fields where it is not easy to defend France's interests," he told Radio Monte Carlo.
The foreign minister's remarks reflected similar statements made on Tuesday by Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

Chirac, speaking just before meeting German Chancellor Helmut Kohl at his Elysee presidential palace on Tuesday evening, said that France could only defend its interests in Europe if it spoke with a single voice.
The conservative president also said he would personally ensure France would meet its European commitments, a clear reference to fulfilling terms for a single European currency.

Opinion polls released at the weekend, prior to an official ban on the publication of such surveys, showed the governing centre-right in the lead in the election but a potential alliance of Socialists, Communists and ecologists gaining ground and within striking distance of a victory.
No more polls will be published before the June 1 conclusion of the two-round election.
De Charette said a leftist win would lead to "confusion within the government and conflict with the president."
"We have several important deadlines ahead of us, concerning European institutional reforms, NATO reforms and enlargement, and European economic and monetary union.
"Can you imagine having a head of state who thinks in one fashion and a prime minister who thinks in another?" he said.

Juppe had warned on Tuesday that a leftist win "would be a shambles in Europe, firstly because the Socialists and Communists don't agree among themselves...and also because the Socialists' economic policy, with extra spending and deficits, would push us off track for European (monetary) union."
A defeat for the government would "spark a crisis in Europe," he had said.

The prime minister said two periods of left-right power sharing in 1986-88 and 1993-95 had shown "cohabitation" between a president and government of opposite parties was "a worst resort", not a recipe for strong government.
But Socialist leader Lionel Jospin brushed off the warnings, saying: "It is obvious France will still speak with a single voice" in case of a left-wing victory.
